title: Scrape charred bits off a griddle over the lip into its grease tray with a scraper
instruction: Scrape the griddle clean into the grease tray with the scraper.
context: Fast food cooks (O*NET 35-2011.00, about 670,000 US jobs, BLS) and restaurant cooks (35-2014.00, about 1.4 million) scrape the griddle between orders and at close. O*NET's tasks for fast food cooks include "Clean food preparation areas, cooking surfaces, and utensils" and "Operate large-volume cooking equipment, such as grills, deep-fat fryers, or griddles"; for restaurant cooks, "Inspect and clean food preparation areas, such as equipment, work surfaces, and serving areas". Charred bits left on the plate burn onto the next order. They are stuck to the plate, so the scraper's edge has to be held flat on the steel and driven into each piece to break it free; a lifted edge rides over it. What it pushes spills round the blade's ends, so strokes have to overlap, and the pile has to be pushed over the lip into the tray, not flicked off onto the line.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. (1) Griddle: a range-top add-on griddle (69 x 31 cm overall; a 56.8 x 31.1 cm cooking surface of 4.6 mm, 7-gauge type 430 stainless; a 7.6 cm grease tray across one end), set on the bench on its own frame with the plate's top 5.0 cm above the bench and clamped down (fixed), tray end toward the robot. The plate runs from x 15.0 (the lip over the tray) to 71.8 and from y -17.55 to 13.55. The tray runs from x 7.4 to 15.0, its floor 3.2 cm below the plate's top. Splash guards stand 5.0 cm above the plate along both sides and the far end. The plate is seasoned and lightly greased, as a working griddle is (in real trials 1.00 g of oil wiped on and buffed off to a film of at most 0.10 g). The griddle's frame sits against two stop blocks on the bench (the plate's near right corner within 2 mm, the lip square within 0.5 degree, the plate's top 5.0 cm up within 2 mm and level). (2) Debris: 88 pieces of charred grease and carbon stuck to the plate, 22.6 g in all (density 1.1 g per cubic cm, compact char). 80 flakes, 7 to 9.5 mm on a side and 2 to 3 mm thick (0.12 to 0.25 g), lie on a 1.2 cm grid over x 16.0 to 28.0, y -10.0 to 6.0 (12 x 16 cm), each turned up to 25 degrees. Eight crusts, 16 to 19 mm on a side and 3 mm thick (0.9 to 1.1 g), lie four to a spot on the two 5 x 5 cm spots where the patties sat, x 19.0 to 24.0, y -8.0 to -3.0 and x 21.0 to 26.0, y 0.0 to 5.0. Each piece is bonded to the plate and comes free when pushed sideways harder than 0.15 N per square cm of its footprint: 0.08 to 0.13 N for a flake, 0.41 to 0.50 N for a crust. Once free it slides on the greased plate. Every piece's size, turn and position is fixed (listed in the task code) and the same every trial. In real trials the debris is made the same way every trial: this layout is printed from the task code and laser-cut as a 3 mm acrylic stencil set flush with the lip and the right guard; flour and water, 1 to 1 by weight, is filled level into its holes (23 mL); the plate is heated on a range away from the robot to 230 degrees C (within 10, at five marked points) for a fixed time and cooled to under 40 degrees C. Each batch is used only if six witness pieces cooked beside it are black through and match, in mass and in black area on the top photo, within 25%, the reference set before the first trial (README). The bond above is how the simulator represents this fresh char; aged, polymerized carbon is out of scope. (3) Scraper: a stiff griddle scraper (the 4 in. size), stainless blade 10.2 cm wide and 1.5 mm thick, 22.0 cm overall, white polypropylene handle 12 x 3.0 x 2.4 cm in line with the blade, 150 g. It lies loose on the bench right of the griddle, edge toward the robot, resting on its edge and the handle's end, centered at x 25.0, y -25.5 (in real trials laid in an outline traced on the bench, within 5 mm and 3 degrees). Both arms start at their ready pose. The griddle is cold (unplugged).
scoring: Measured by mass, as shares of the 22.6 g of debris, from where each piece ends up. In the tray means inside the tray's walls and below the plate's top. Off the griddle means outside its footprint (plate, tray and splash guards): on the bench, the floor, or carried off on the scraper. Every other piece is left on the griddle. The trial scores 1.0 when at least 98% is in the tray and at most 1% is left on the griddle (the plate is clean: 1% is about one small flake), and the scraper has been set down on the bench off the griddle, released and still for 1 s. Set down: the point where its neck meets the handle less than 3 cm above the bench and outside the griddle's footprint; released: no gripper touching it; still: under 1 cm a second and 10 degrees a second. The job is not finished while the scraper is still in hand or lying on the griddle. It scores 0.75 when at least 90% is in the tray and at most 5% is left on the griddle (5% is about one crust). It scores 0.5 when at least 60% is in the tray (most of the area done), and 0.25 when at least 25% is (a first strip cleared). Otherwise it scores 0. Doing nothing scores 0. Two caps apply to every score. More than 2% off the griddle (about 0.45 g, a few flakes thrown onto the line) caps the score at 0.25. A gouge caps it at 0.5 for the rest of the trial: while the scraper is held and sliding with its edge on the plate (within 0.6 mm, about the simulator's resting gap), the blade over 70 degrees to the plate, or its edge tilted over 10 degrees so only one corner touches, for 1 cm or more of a stroke (a stand-in for chatter marks in the seasoning). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. In a real trial the same shares are weighed on a 0.01 g scale: the tray's gain (in the tray); what is lifted off the plate, guards and blade with a razor scraper and brush (left on the griddle); what is brushed off the catch sheets, bench, floor and scraper (off the griddle). Their sum is the total; a trial whose total is more than 10% off the batch's expected mass is repeated. The set-down is judged from the video. Top photos before and after, from a fixed camera under a fixed raking light with a 1 cm grid, record what is left; a new scratch 1 cm or longer is the gouge.
reset_notes: Empty, wash, dry and weigh the tray. Scrape, wipe and dry the plate until its grid photo shows no particle 1 mm or larger (re-season every 10 trials). Re-grease (1.00 g of oil buffed to at most 0.10 g), stencil and cook a fresh batch, cool it to under 40 degrees C and accept it on its witness check (README). Clamp the griddle against its stops and lay the scraper in its outline. In simulation every trial starts with every piece bonded in place and the tray empty.
fidelity: Real size. Each piece is a rigid box held by a breakable joint, freed when the blade pushes past its bond: 11 to 28 N per m of edge (baked food soils on steel: 0.3 to 80 J/m2), standing in for the real trials' charred paste, whose bond is measured each batch. Sim char 22.6 g (compact), real about 12 g (estimated); both scored by share. Real flakes are irregular and crumble. Friction: greased plate 0.15 to 0.2, carbon on steel 0.4 to 0.5. No heat. Rigid scraper. Gouge: a blade-angle rule.
